decisions.reason: SOL keeps the departure and mass of mourners while using natural phrasing.
“Those who departed” preserves the Korean euphemism; “the dead” makes it explicit.
SOL keeps the arriving family members and makes the sentence flow naturally.
The envoy’s introduction carries the message; SOL preserves the scene without the redundant sequencing.
The fragment naturally completes the preceding sentence and keeps the focus on Jin Wikyung.
“The envoy” refers clearly to the Murim Alliance envoy just introduced, and “calmly led” keeps his composed manner.
SOL preserves the invitation and rest after the journey in natural dialogue.
SOL keeps the envoy’s gratitude and respectful address.
The Korean explicitly names the Jin Family of Taiyuan; SOL drops the established full name.
SOL preserves the contrast without changing the envoy’s genuine respect.
“Carried a special weight” conveys the significance of the title naturally.
The Korean says “I, too”; SOL drops that explicit sense of shared feeling.
SOL preserves that he is no longer either role while giving the contrast a natural cadence.
SOL keeps both his provincial standing and recognition as another Alliance Leader.
SOL keeps the silent look and turn away in brisk, natural prose.
The Korean explicitly has Hyuk Mujin tilt his head before hurrying after the narrator; SOL preserves both actions.
“Rain of petals” keeps the image and reads naturally.
“The people” is a natural rendering of the people known among the family and preserves their virtue.
“Resolve to protect” preserves the Jin Family’s righteous purpose in protecting the land and its people.
“Come together and grown stronger” preserves the family’s unity and renewed strength.
SOL preserves the window’s unusual length, the palpable changes, and its customary closing.
“The one thing” keeps the unease focused on the lack of a follow-up Quest.
“Would happen” preserves the narrator’s expectation of another event.
SOL changes deaths being inevitable into someone always dying, and adds that the burden grew with every death.
“All of Murim” naturally preserves the crisis hanging over the whole martial world.
The Korean specifies four Demon Lords in addition to the Demon Empress; SOL changes the count to three.
The contraction keeps the sense of locally recruited forces in natural narration.
SOL adds “their own forces,” narrowing the source’s unspecified subject without support.
The Korean says his steps had been moving unconsciously before he stopped; SOL drops that detail.
“You all” preserves the plural addressee in the Korean.
The Korean refers to one carefully prepared plan; SOL changes it to plural plans.
“Without explaining them” preserves that he died without revealing their meaning.
SOL preserves the spear strike, the days since the fighting ended, and the narrator’s clear memory.
The fragment preserves the calm voice and expression as a concise continuation.
The contraction preserves the Demon Lord’s proof of his readiness to die.
“Facing certain death” naturally preserves the source’s inevitable death.
SOL naturally conveys a life whose end the person chose and the claim that they do not lie.
“Tone and manner” preserves the clues in his words and demeanor; “some idea” fits the narrator’s inference.
The singular “it” correctly refers to the possibility that seemed unrealistic.
The past perfect keeps Jeok Cheongang’s answer in the earlier conversation.
“People like them” avoids adding a gender restriction while keeping the insult and meaning.
The added connective keeps the narrator’s natural self-questioning without changing the questions.
“Bullshit” preserves the vulgar, dismissive force of the Korean.
The Korean image is of clinging to an endless chain of thoughts; “wrestled with” replaces that image.
